nodes.label: Circular procurement policies

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_000
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How does the combination of different policy mechanisms contribute to the development of policies for FTI products and circular economy characteristics?
nodes.answer: The combination of different policy mechanisms takes into account the coerciveness of policies and the purpose of policies, reflecting the life cycle of FTI products and specific CE characteristics such as CE strategies, loops, sociotechnical elements, and circular business models.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_001
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: In terms of resource life cycle, which phases do restrictive policies primarily target?
nodes.answer: Restrictive policies primarily target the head of the resource life cycle, the Sourcing and Production phase, and the tail of the resource life cycle, the Collection and Recovery phase, with fewer policies addressing the Pre-Consumption and Consumption phases.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_002
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How do the policies within the six life cycle phases in the circular policy canvas prioritize between the outer loop (recycling) and the inner loop (reuse)?
nodes.answer: The policies within the six life cycle phases in the circular policy canvas are more concentrated in the outer loop (recycling) with 15 policies addressing it, while only 10 policies focus on the inner loop (reuse).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_003
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What are some examples of more established policies found in the outer loop of the circular policy canvas?
nodes.answer: Examples of more established policies found in the outer loop of the circular policy canvas include Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), separate textile waste collection, and the EU Eco label.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_004
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: How do the value-entered policies in the Sourcing and Production phase aim to tackle the linear economy?
nodes.answer: The value-entered policies in this phase aim to penalize the linear economy through taxes on carbon production and material usage, as well as bans on planned obsolescence business models.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_005
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What do policies targeting the Sourcing and Production phase of the circular economy focus on?
nodes.answer: Policies targeting the Sourcing and Production phase primarily focus on resource and value.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_006
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the significance of mapping CE policies related to FTI on the Circular Policy Canvas?
nodes.answer: Mapping CE policies on the Circular Policy Canvas helps identify gaps in the EU policy approach towards FTI, presenting opportunities for policy improvement and enhancement.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_007
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What challenges exist in mapping all related policies for circularity, as noted by Auto and Lazaretto (2020)?
nodes.answer: Auto and Lazaretto (2020) highlight that mapping all related policies for circularity is a massive task due to potential unforeseen interactions between policies. Sectoral policies often lack consideration for interactions with other waste streams, industries, and resources, creating complexity for comprehensive mapping efforts.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Circular economy practices|Circular procurement policies_qna_008
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What is the classification rationale for the policy on unsold good destruction disclosure and ban?
nodes.answer: The classification rationale for this policy includes the restrictive nature of banning a linear economy practice, its focus on the pre-consumption phase of the resource life cycle, its placement in the outer loop of the circular economy for recycling, its narrow strategy to limit wasted resources, and its emphasis on data disclosure.
